1.1.title: Background
1.1.text: Most large applications today are built as many small services that talk to each other over the network. A shopping site, for example, has separate services for the catalogue, the cart, payment, shipping and orders, each with its own database or cache [1]. This style allows teams to deploy and scale each piece independently. It also creates a kind of failure that a single program does not have: a fault does not stay where it starts. Take a slow database. The service that queries it starts waiting, so it answers slowly. The services that call that service begin to time out, retry, and add load on top of load. Within a minute, a dozen services are raising alarms together, and the operator on call is looking at a wall of red where the first thing that broke is no louder than the things it broke. Practitioners call this an alert storm. The real cost is not the number of alerts but the time spent deciding which one deserves action [2, 3]. Two facts make the problem manageable. First, trouble travels along the call graph: from a callee to the services that wait on it, not in random directions. Second, it travels probabilistically. A caller that has a timeout, a cache, or a circuit breaker may live through a failing dependency; a caller without those protections will not. A tool that knows the call graph and how likely trouble is to cross each edge can answer two questions that a ranked list of alarms cannot: which service is the origin, and which healthy services are about to be pulled in. Recent research answers the first question with heavy machinery: models that fuse metrics, traces, and logs into learned representations and localise the fault with graph neural networks [4, 5, 6]. They work, but they need labelled failure data that most teams do not have, they need accelerated hardware at inference time, and their output (a cluster number, an embedding ranking) cannot be checked by the engineer against the numbers on the dashboard. Classic observability products, on the other hand, usually ask for changes inside the application, such as client libraries, agents, or a sidecar in every pod, before they show anything. This project takes a different route. It watches the containers from outside, over SSH and the Docker socket, so that nothing in the monitored system is modified. From these observations, it builds a live dependency graph, and on top of that graph, it runs an unsupervised, a single-core diagnosis pipeline that proposes a root cause, a prediction of what will fail next, a fault type, and a short runbook, each backed by numbers for the operator to inspect.

1.2.title: Problem Statement
1.2.text: The project addresses four linked problems that a team running containerised microservices encounters in practice: • Invisible dependencies. The real call graph of a running system is rarely documented and drifts over time. Compose files list what was declared, not what is actually communicating. Without instrumentation, no one can say which service calls which, or in which direction. • Alert storms. When one service fails, its callers fail too. Ranking alarms by severity often points to the loudest service, which is often a victim and not the cause. • No view of what comes next. Operators learn that a service is affected only after it alarms. A model of how failure spreads on this particular system could warn earlier. • Black-box diagnosis. Methods that need training data and return an opaque score are hard to trust at three in the morning. An engineer needs to see the evidence and how it was combined. The problem is therefore to observe a containerised system without touching it, recover its call graph, detect trouble per service against that service’s own normal, rank the likely origin of an incident, predict how it will spread, and show every step in a form an engineer can verify, with no labelled data and no specialised hardware.

1.3.title: Motivation and Need for the Project
1.3.text: Small teams and student projects run exactly the systems for which heavyweight AIOps products are a poor fit: a handful of Docker hosts on a cloud account, no budget for per-host licences, and applications that nobody wants to re-instrument. Yet, these systems fail in the same cascading way as larger ones. We saw it ourselves while running the benchmark applications for this project: killing one datastore container produced alarms on the services that call it within seconds. Three observations shaped the work. First, much of what an operator needs is already visible from the host: container state, CPU and memory against the container’s own limits, network counters, and the table of open TCP sockets inside each container. Second, a per-service model of ‘normal’ removes the need for global thresholds, which fail because services differ by orders of magnitude in every metric. Third, a result that cannot be reproduced or audited data is of little use if the evaluation is not as careful as the tool itself: ground truth that the detector never sees, confidence intervals, paired tests, and an honest account of what did not work.

1.4.title: Objectives
1.4.text: 1. To build a platform that connects to Docker hosts over SSH, discovers the service topology, and shows live health, metrics and dependencies in a 2D and a 3D view, without changing the monitored applications. 2. To recover call directions from observed sockets, and where names carry no information, from the services' own behaviour. 3. To detect trouble per service against its own recent history with a hybrid of a learned detector (Isolation Forest) and a robust statistical rule layer, treating container facts such as “stopped” or “crash-looping” as evidence rather than a degree. 4. To rank the root cause of an incident by separating a service’s own deviation from what its neighbours explain, and by running a random walk over the call graph. 5. To model cascading failure with learned per-edge propagation probabilities, predict which services are next, and warn early about gradual faults. 6. To classify the fault type and attach a short runbook, so the output is something an engineer can act on. 7. To make the three engines (Rules, ML, Hybrid) switchable and to show, side by side and on the same readings, what each one detects, computes, and predicts. 8. To evaluate all of this on real and synthetic fault campaigns with ground truth that the detector never sees, reporting confidence intervals, paired tests, an ablation, and the negative results.

1.5.title: Scope of the Project
1.5.text: The system targets Docker-based microservice stacks on Linux hosts that can be reached over SSH. It reads container state, statistics, and socket tables; it does not read application payloads and does not require code changes. It was developed and measured on the following applications: • ShopFlow, a 13-service retail checkout system, and LedgerLine, a 12-service retail-banking transfer system. Both were built for this study as test benches, each on its own EC2 host with its own Fault Lab and a Prometheus–Grafana–Loki monitoring stack (Section 5.10); both were run under open-loop traffic for 217 minutes with 62 faults injected; • Sock Shop, the open microservices demo, used for development; • a social-network application from the DeathStarBench suite [7] (27 containers), and the OpenTelemetry demo, used to check that discovery works on third-party systems; • a synthetic generator that writes runs in the same recorded format over 16 random topologies, used to enlarge the evaluation. The mapper is not a distributed tracing tool: it does not include request identifiers or spans, and the “Traces” page displays sampled TCP connection snapshots. It does not replace an application performance monitoring suite. No language model is involved in the diagnosis; the “assistant” is a transparent composition of statistical models, and Chapter 7 discusses where a language-model agent could be added.

1.6.title: Significance and Expected Contribution
1.6.text: The project demonstrates that useful root-cause analysis does not require instrumentation, labels, or a GPU, and it measures how far this approach can go. Its contributions are: • an instrumentation-free observation layer that recovers topology and call direction from container sockets and Docker state; • a probabilistic cascading-failure model whose per-edge propagation probabilities are Beta–Binomial posteriors learned online from the system’s own incidents, with risk flowing over the graph by noisy-OR; • a hybrid detector in which a per-service Isolation Forest and a robust rule layer jointly raise the alarm and container facts count as evidence, with an operating contract that reports alarm time as well as false-alarm episodes; • a fact-aware, decomposition-based ranker for the root cause, and call directions learned from telemetry; • a Detection engines page that runs Rules, ML and Hybrid in parallel and shows what each detected, computed and predicted; • a reproducible evaluation with a blind fault injector, a held-out synthetic benchmark, bootstrap intervals, paired tests, an ablation and an amplification study, together with the results that did not help and a measurement bug that had hidden half of the real faults; • a working platform of about 36 000 lines of TypeScript with 329 automated tests, a traffic generator and a host-check tool, used throughout the experiments.

1.7.title: Organization of the Report
1.7.text: Chapter 2 reviews related work on anomaly detection, root-cause localisation, cascade modelling, and observability tooling, and states the gap. Chapter 3 formulates the problem and presents the proposed system, its architecture, and its two agents. Chapter 4 describes the methodology: the models, the evaluation measures, the blind fault injector, and the statistics. Chapter 5 describes the implementation: the modules, interfaces, core code, algorithms, configuration, the prototype, and testing. Chapter 6 reports the results of the experiments, the comparison with existing approaches, and the operational findings from the hosts. Chapter 7 concludes and lists limitations and future work. The appendices provide the configuration constants, the fault classes, the test suites, and a short user guide.

2.1.title: Introduction
2.1.text: This project draws on five bodies of work: anomaly detection on time series, root-cause localisation in microservice systems, models of how failure spreads, evaluation practices for anomaly and diagnosis methods, and the observability tools that supply the data. Each statement about a cited work below restates what that work documents; where we compare, we specify what we compared.

2.2.1.title: Anomaly detection
2.2.1.text: Isolation Forest [8, 9] isolates an outlier with few random cuts and requires no density estimate, making it suitable for per-service streams of mixed and skewed metrics. Distance and density methods [10, 11], the histogram-based score HBOS [12] and the multivariate control chart of Hotelling [13, 14] with a shrinkage covariance estimate [15] are natural alternatives, and we compare all of them in Chapter 6. Robust location and scale from the median and the median absolute deviation [16, 17] underpin the rule layer of the proposed system. Surveys of streaming and learned anomaly detection [18, 19, 20] and deployed detectors for monitoring data [21, 22] describe the setting we work in: unlabelled streams, drifting baselines, and a high cost of false alarms.

2.2.2.title: Evaluation of anomaly detectors
2.2.2.text: Several studies criticise the common practice of scoring anomaly detectors point by point, with an adjustment that credits a whole event if any point inside it is flagged [23, 24], and argue for range-based precision and recall that respect the duration of an event [25]. This is why the evaluation in Chapter 4 is event-level: a fault counts as detected only when an alarm names a truly involved service while the fault is active, and false alarms are counted as episodes outside every fault window.

2.2.3.title: Root-cause localisation in microservices
2.2.3.text: MonitorRank [26] introduced a personalised random walk over the call graph, biased by how anomalous each service looks, and ranks the services by the walk’s stationary share. MicroRCA [27], CloudRanger [28], Microscope [29], AutoMAP [30] and MicroRank [31] extend this idea with anomaly-weighted transitions, causal-graph construction and trace spectra. Causal approaches recover structure using the PC algorithm or hierarchical discovery [32, 33, 34]. Learned methods localise with graph autoencoders and multi-source fusion of metrics, traces and logs [5, 4, 6, 35]. A survey of AIOps approaches to failure management [3] and one specific to anomaly and root-cause work in microservices [36] place these methods in context. Most of them require traces, labelled failures or training, and some need accelerated hardware; the random-walk family, however, needs only the call graph and an anomaly score, which is the basis for this project.

2.2.4.title: Cascading failure and change detection
2.2.4.text: The independent-cascade model of influence spread [37] forms the basis of our propagation model, with edge probabilities estimated online rather than assumed. Probabilistic forecasts are assessed using proper scoring rules, reliability diagrams, and expected calibration error [38, 39, 40]. Detection latency can be addressed with classical change-point detection [41, 42]. PageRank [43] and reciprocal-rank fusion [44] inform ranking; Granger causality [45] and transfer entropy [46] inform the study of call direction; random forests and CART [47, 48] support the fault-type classifier.

2.2.5.title: Benchmarks and chaos engineering
2.2.5.text: Open benchmark applications such as DeathStarBench [7] and Train-Ticket [49] provide realistic microservice systems to test on, and chaos-engineering practice [50] provides the method for injecting faults on purpose. Our fault injector follows that practice but, importantly, keeps its ledger private: nothing inside the system under test is labelled.

2.2.6.title: Observability tooling
2.2.6.text: Production observability usually combines three kinds of tools. Metric systems scrape numbers from endpoints that each service exposes. Distributed tracing follows a request across services and needs the application, or a proxy in front of it, to propagate trace identifiers. Application performance monitoring products add agents inside the runtime. All three give an accurate picture once the instrumentation exists; none works on a stack that nobody is willing to modify. Service meshes can supply topology without code changes, but they require a sidecar in every pod. The site-reliability literature [2] is clear. That the hard part is not collecting signals but deciding what to look at first, which is the gap that root-cause ranking aims to address. 2.4.text: Four gaps motivate the design. 1. Observation without instrumentation. The graph that random-walk and causal methods assume is usually given. 2.5.title: Summary
2.5.text: Existing root-cause methods are strong on accuracy but assume instrumentation, labels or hardware that small teams do not have, and they are usually evaluated optimistically. The proposed system occupies a different point in the design space: it is instrumentation-free, unsupervised, auditable, and honest about its limits. The next chapter will formulate the problem and describe the system.

3.1.title: Problem Formulation
3.1.text: A system is a set S of N services with a directed call graph. An edge u →v means that u calls v, so a failure travels against the arrow, from v to the callers that wait on it. Every ∆= 5 s the collector produces, for each service s, a reading xs(t) (R { })8, holding CPU, memory, CPU throttling, network in and out, request rate, error share and 95th-percentile latency. The symbol marks a metric that was not reported. It is never replaced by zero, as a stopped container must be distinguishable from an idle one. Each reading comes with a container state (running, paused, restarting, exited, detached). At time t, the pipeline must decide four things, using only readings up to t: (i) whether an incident is in progress; (ii) which service is the root cause; (iii) which currently healthy services will be affected before the incident ends; (iv) what kind of fault it is. The pipeline must achieve this without labelled failures, without modifying any application, and fast enough for the decision window to finish well inside the 5 s collection period.

3.2.title: Proposed Solution
3.2.text: The proposed system is an agent-assisted pipeline in a concrete sense. A collector agent observes the containers from outside the application. A diagnosis assistant turns those observations into a cause, a forecast of what will fail next, a fault type, a runbook, and an explanation the operator can check. Between the two sits the evidence-weighted dependency graph. Figure 3.1 shows the whole system, and Figure 3.2 illustrates one 5-second cycle. The solution has seven steps, each described in Chapter 4. 1. Observe. Read container state, statistics and socket tables over SSH; install nothing on the host. 2. Build the graph. Merge declared dependencies (from the Compose file) with observed ones; orient each observed socket by the listening port; assign a confidence and a dependency share to each edge. 3. Learn directions. Where the heuristic cannot determine who calls whom, vote over dynamic and structural signals. 4. Detect. Judge every service against its own recent past with two Isolation Forests and a robust rule layer; treat container facts as evidence. 5. Rank. Split each service’s deviation into what its callees explain and what they do not; run a personalised random walk over the call graph; present facts first. 6. Predict. Spread risk over the graph by using noisy-OR with edge probabilities learned from the system's own incidents; warn early about gradual faults. 7. Diagnose and explain. Classify the fault type, attach a short runbook, and show the evidence behind every number. 3.4.text: The architecture has five layers (Figure 3.1). Dashboard. A React 19 application built with Vite. It contains no polling logic: the server pushes graph and incident updates over a WebSocket, and REST calls fetch history and configuration. The views are described in Section 5.7. Server. A Node.js process (Express 5, TypeScript) that owns all state and is the only component that writes to disk. The GraphStore keeps nodes, edges, and targets; the MetricStore keeps a ring buffer of readings per service; the TraceStore keeps connection events; the IncidentManager drives the engines and turns their verdicts into incidents. Connection and collection. A connection manager keeps one SSH session per target and runs commands from a fixed catalogue (e.g., `docker ps`, `inspect`, `stats`, `logs`, and reads of `/proc/<pid>/net/tcp`). 4.1.title: Objective of the Study
4.1.text: The study asks how far an instrumentation-free, unsupervised pipeline can go in answering four operational questions about a running microservice system: is something wrong, where did it start, who is next, and what kind of fault is it. It also asks, with equal weight, how reliable the answers are. On the synthetic track, the settings were chosen on a tuning split kept apart from the data used for the reported numbers; on the real track, they were not tuned on a held-out system, and the report states this where it matters.

4.2.title: Method and Approach
4.2.text: The approach is a pipeline of small, separately testable models rather than one large model. Each stage has a stated input, a stated output, and a measured contribution (Section 6.1.4). The pipeline is built in this order: 1. an evidence-weighted graph from observed sockets and declared dependencies; 2. learned call directions for pairs the heuristic cannot orient; 3. a hybrid detector combining per-service Isolation Forests with a robust rule layer, incorporating container facts; 4. a ranker built on a deviation decomposition and a personalised random walk; 5. a cascade model with Beta–Binomial edge probabilities and noisy-OR risk, plus trend-based early warning and change-point alarms; 6. a fault-type classifier and runbook. The evaluation then replays recorded runs through the engines and scores them against a ledger that the engines never see.

4.6.1.title: The evidence-weighted graph
4.6.1.text: Each edge has a confidence \( c(e) \), the strongest evidence behind it: 1.0 for a call seen in request logs or oriented by a listening port, 0.85 when oriented only by the ephemeral-port range, 0.70 when observed with no direction evidence, 0.50 when the direction is unresolved, and 0.40 when declared in the Compose file but never seen carrying traffic. The dependency share \( d(e) \) of an edge leaving a caller is its slow-baseline traffic normalised over the caller’s edges. A slow baseline is used because a link goes quiet exactly when its callee dies; weighting on the instantaneous rate would make a dead dependency look less and less important. 4.6.2.title: Learned call directions
4.6.2.text: The collector sees most pairs from both ends (in the recorded runs 15 of 32 pairs in one system and 18 of 36 in the other), so direction must be recovered before a walk can follow it. The shipped heuristic reads names (an entry point calls a service, a service calls a datastore) and fails when names carry no role. We instead learn the direction of each observed pair online from the services’ own histories, with no labels and no names. Four dynamic signals use what services do during trouble: upward symptoms, downward traffic drops, implication (P(Ta | Tb) −P(Tb | Ta), with T meaning “in trouble”), and a Granger-style F-test on the symptom series. Two structural signals use the observed graph: the depth of each service from the entry point, and whether a service reports request metrics of its own (a datastore does not). The learned direction is the sign of ∑m ωmsm(a,b) with weights ωm {0.5,1,2} chosen by grid search on the tuning split. A pair is left undecided if the magnitude is below 0.05.

4.6.3.title: Per-service Isolation Forests
4.6.3.text: A service is judged against its own recent past, never against a global threshold, because services differ by orders of magnitude in every metric. The eight features are split into two groups, each with its own forest of 100 trees trained on a sliding window of the last W = 120 readings judged normal: own (CPU, memory, throttling), which a dependency cannot cause, and symptom (traffic, errors, latency, network), which can be inherited. A reading is scored by the forest built before it arrived. With \( E[h(x)] \) the mean path length. and c(ψ) the usual normaliser, the raw score s(x) = 2−E[h(x)]/c(ψ) becomes a level level(x) = s(x)−˜s ℓ−˜s , ℓ= ˜s+κ ·1.4826·MAD(strain), (4.1) Where \(\tilde{s}\) is the median training score and \(\kappa = 3\). Level 1 is the service’s own alarm line. Only readings with a level below one join the training window, so a fault never becomes the baseline. Four refinements were each found by testing and are ablated in Section 6.1.4. • training jitter at each feature’s floor, so that a feature that never moved can still register a later jump; • a range guard counting floors beyond the training range, because a forest scores an out-of-range value no higher than its most extreme training point; • one-sided features: less CPU, memory, throttling, error or latency than usual is never a fault of the service itself (it happens after every restart); • two-speed drift: a small steady shift (level < 3) is accepted as the new normal within two minutes, a large one is quarantined for thirty minutes.

4.6.4.title: Rules and container facts
4.6.4.text: A robust one-sided z-score per metric (median and MAD, bad direction only) gives a rule score ρs normalised so that 1 is its three-sigma line. A container that is exited, paused, restarting, or network-detached is a fact: evidence, not degree. Two facts that raw container state misses were added after inspecting the real runs. A docker stop exits with code zero, which looks like a finished job, so a service that had been running and then exits is considered stopped. A crash loop looks healthy between kills, so two outages within three minutes mark it.

4.6.5.text: Let \(\lambda_s\) be a service’s forest level, and \(f_s \in \{0,1\}\) its fact flag. 4.6.8.title: Early warning, change points and fault typing
4.6.8.text: For each rising-only feature, a least-squares line is fitted over the last two minutes and projected two minutes ahead through the range guard; a service not yet at the alarm level whose trend will reach it is flagged. Separately, online Page–Hinkley change-point detection [41] on the raw metrics can raise the alarm before the forest line is crossed. At the alarm, 35 features of the top suspect’s telemetry (container-state history, exit code, number of separate outages, memory slope, CPU and throttling change, latency and error ratios against a pre-fault baseline, network drop, number of anomalous callers) are input into a random forest [47] that names the fault type (crash, stop, pause, crash-loop, flap, memory, brownout, latency, partition). A short runbook of two to four concrete checks per type is attached. This layer changes neither detection nor ranking.

4.8.title: Data Processing and Analysis
4.8.text: Readings keep missing values as missing. Each recorded trace stores, per window, the readings, container facts and the engine inputs, so the engines can be replayed deterministically. Warm-up (the first five minutes of each run) is excluded from false-alarm and ROC counts. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals over faults [51]; comparisons between engines are paired bootstrap differences over the same faults, with two-sided p-values; seed-averaged results are means over seeds. Overlapping faults within a run are not independent, so intervals are, if anything, optimistic. With 62 real faults, a difference below about 8 points cannot be resolved, and no claim is made below that.

4.10.1.title: Systems and traffic
4.10.1.text: Two containerised applications were built for the study. ShopFlow is a 13-service retail checkout system (HTTP fan-out, two PostgreSQL instances, two Redis caches, a NATS consumer). LedgerLine is a 12-service retail-banking transfer system (a saga orchestrator, a double-entry ledger, a third-party FX provider, a batch worker). Both ran for 217 minutes. Under open-loop traffic with a daily wave, bursts, and flash crowds, each scenario has its own EC2 host, Fault Lab, and Grafana (Section 5.10).

4.10.2.title: Blind fault injection
4.10.2.text: Faults arrive by a non-homogeneous Poisson process whose rate follows the load, each with a class, a role-weighted target, a heavy-tailed duration and a severity; with some probability, a follower is spawned in the target's one-hop neighbourhood, so incidents overlap. Faults are physical (SIGKILL, pause, cgroup CPU and memory limits, network detach) and nothing is labelled inside the system under test. The injector writes a private ledger with, per fault, the true root cause and the services structurally able to be affected; this ledger is read only after the run. The two systems contribute 62 faults over seven classes (Figure 4.2). The ledger is written by the injector and read only when scoring.

4.10.3.title: Synthetic benchmark
4.10.3.text: To enlarge the sample, a generator writes runs in the identical recorded format: the two topologies with their measured per-service baselines, plus random topologies, nine fault classes that propagate up and down the graph, overlapping faults, and unlabelled noise (noisy neighbours, deploys, missing readings). Settings were chosen on a 16-campaign tuning split (170 faults, seed 1), and every reported synthetic number comes from a disjoint 16-campaign split (178 faults, seed 2) scored once. The generator also takes an amplification factor A, which scales how strongly callers feel a fault (retry storms), and a class filter; it underlies the amplification study.

4.10.4.title: Questions the evaluation answers
4.10.4.text: Q1. Does the hybrid name the true cause more often than the rule layer, and how does it compare with ranking by anomaly alone and with the ML engine? Q2. Which detector separates faulted from healthy services best, and is the Isolation Forest worth keeping? Q3. How much does each mechanism contribute (ablation), and does graph-aware ranking help when victims are louder than the cause (amplification)? Q4. Do learned propagation probabilities predict cascades better than fixed ones, and are they calibrated? Q5. Do learned directions remain correct when names carry no information, and do change-point alarms reduce detection delay?

4.10.5.title: A measurement bug
4.10.5.text: Each recorded run contains two fault campaigns that both number their faults from one. The ledger reader kept only the second, hiding 14 of 31 faults per system for every engine and counted their outages as false alarms. We fixed the reader, added a regression test, and now every number in this report uses all 62 faults.

5.2.8.title: Incidents
5.2.8.text: The incident manager, once per target per cycle, runs the three engines' shared step, builds the evidence for the active engine, calls the root-cause engine, and either updates the open incident or opens a new one. A new incident takes the status DEGRADED or INCIDENT according to whether any service is critical (Figure 3.5); it is resolved when the alarm clears. Severity is raised when more than a configured number of services are critical, and lowered for a service that nothing depends on and that depends on nothing, which has no blast radius.

5.8.title: Security Considerations
5.8.text: The tool maintains SSH access to hosts, so it was designed to expose as little as possible. • Keys stay on the operator’s machine. The configuration stores only the path of the key file. Private keys are never copied into the repository, and *.pem files are git-ignored as a backstop. • A fixed command catalogue. Every command the server can run on a host is built by a function in one file, and every argument that reaches a shell is checked against the shapes Docker itself produces (container identifiers, timestamps, tail lengths, paths). A test ensures that an identifier with shell metacharacters is refused before a command is built. • Bounded output and time. Each command has a timeout and a maximum output size, so a misbehaving host cannot make the server wait or buffer without limit. • Local control surfaces. The Fault Lab panel listens on localhost only, and its requests need a header that the page itself sets. Grafana and Prometheus also listen on localhost and are reached through an SSH tunnel. • Ingest token. The push endpoint is protected by a token. The built-in default is for local use and must be changed if the server can be reached by others. • One write per host. The only change the mapper makes on a host is restarting a container that exited with a non-zero code, with a few attempts at most per container, never for load generators, and is switched off with MAPPER_AUTO_RESTART=off. • Load limits. The traffic generator clamps the number of virtual users to a fixed ceiling and only starts from the traffic controller.

5.10.1.title: Monitoring: Prometheus, Grafana and Loki
5.10.1.text: Each bench carries a monitoring stack that is deliberately a separate Compose project. The application project stays exactly as a mapper should discover it, and monitoring can be started and stopped independently. The stack includes Prometheus (with 24-hour retention), Grafana with a provisioned dashboard, Loki with Promtail shipping every container’s logs, and a small exporter that reads per-container CPU, memory, network, restarts, out-of-memory kills, and health from the Docker API (the same numbers as docker stats). A “dashboard viewer” container queries Grafana every few seconds, as a person would, so that those links are live and visible to a mapper. Everything listens on localhost; Grafana is reached through an SSH tunnel. Figures 5.16 and 5.17 show the provisioned dashboard of each bench: health at a glance (request rate, 5xx ratio, p95 latency, containers running, restarts, memory), request metrics from each service’s own endpoint, container metrics from the Docker API, and application internals (database pool waits, unconsumed events, process memory, heap). Grafana serves two purposes in the study. It is the operator’s ordinary view of a healthy and a faulted bench, and it is a second, independent source against which the mapper’s readings can be compared on the same time axis.

5.10.2.title: Traffic
5.10.2.text: Each bench has an always-on, open-loop traffic generator. The default mode is organic: visitor sessions with think times, popular products, returning users, and a day-and-night wave (about twelve workers); a steady mode gives a flat load. A quiet mode stops the generator so that only a person’s own clicks reach the gateway. ShopFlow also has a storefront that can be used like a customer, with a live request log and an “autopilot” that browses by itself.

5.10.3.title: The Fault Lab
5.10.3.text: The Fault Lab (lab/faultlab in each bench repository) is the fault injector for the evaluation. Its properties are those the methodology requires. • Blind. The mapper is never told what is injected. Everything the injector does is written to a private ledger, which is read only when scoring. • Physical faults act on containers: SIGKILL with the restart policy bringing the service back (crash), repeated kills (crash-loop), docker stop, pause, resource limits (brownout, memory), network detach (partition), and repeated pause-and-release cycles (flap). • Organic and reproducible. A campaign draws faults from a Poisson process with a profile, a duration, a rate, a maximum number at once, and an optional seed; the same seed gives the same campaign. • Targeted. The operator may restrict the fault types and services that may be hit, or inject one fault by hand with a severity and a hold time, and heal everything at once. 5.11.title: Host and Mapper Diagnostic Tools
5.11.text: Two tools were added after operating the benchmark hosts showed that "nothing appears in the dashboard" has two very different causes: the host cannot answer, or the mapper has a problem. npm run check-host walks one instance step by step and stops at the first failure: whether port 22 answers; whether the key exists with permissions SSH accepts; whether login works; the host’s memory, load, and disk; whether Docker answers within 25 seconds and which containers run; whether the application answers on its port; which peers each front-end container calls and whether they are other containers; and whether the mapper server is up. Each failure indicates which side to look at. npm run mapper-edges prints what the running mapper holds for a project or service: the target’s status and last-seen time, the matching nodes and their status, and every edge in or out with its evidence and last-seen time. Together, the two tools can separate a host problem from a mapper problem in minutes.

6.1.2.title: Which detector
6.1.2.text: Figure 6.4 and Table 6.3 score each detector as a service-level classifier. 6.1.3.title: Detection delay and root-cause depth
6.1.3.text: Figure 6.5 shows detection delay as a cumulative distribution. On the real systems the change-point alarm lifts the detected fraction from 90% to 95% and moves the median from 10.5 s to 4.9 s; on the synthetic set, whose faults are abrupt, the curves almost coincide. Figure 6.6 shows the true cause in the top k: the ML-based rankers reach it first more often than the rules on the real systems, and the curves converge by k = 2 to 3 near the 90% detection ceiling, so the remaining misses are mostly faults the engine does not see (brownouts on near-idle services) rather than faults it ranks badly.

6.1.4.title: Ablation
6.1.4.text: Figure 6.7 removes one mechanism at a time. The most important single component is the docker stop fact: without it C+N falls by 19 points on the real systems and 16 on the synthetic set, because every stopped service goes unnamed. The crash-loop fact (3 and 7 points), the range guard (4 and 11 points) and the random walk (3 and 1 points) each contribute. Two mechanisms act on the contract rather than on accuracy. Removing the one-sided features raises alarm time on the real systems from 5% to 30%. Alarming at level one instead of two raises it to 22% and false alarms to 11.3 per hour while changing C+N by only +2 points. The one-sided features do not matter on the synthetic set, where restarts do not lower memory: an effect of the real systems that the simulator does not reproduce.

6.1.9.title: Cost
6.1.9.text: The pipeline is unsupervised, needs no GPU and runs on one core. In a single replay, The two real systems (12 and 13 services) share one decision window, covering the per-service area. 6.1.12.title: Operational findings from the benchmark hosts
6.1.12.text: Operating the benchmark hosts produced three findings that changed the tools. A host too small for its workload looks like a mapper fault. The OpenTelemetry demo ran on a 2-vCPU, 4 GiB instance, with a load average of about 25 and 3.6 of 3.8 GiB of memory in use, no swap, and Docker did not answer within 25 seconds; the dashboard showed no services. A second host with 4 GiB of swap and a load average of 0.2 ran 27 containers of a social-network benchmark normally. The lesson is operational: the mapper depends on the host’s Docker daemon answering, and a host that cannot answer shows nothing. The check tool now says so in one step. • Idle front ends have no edges. On a healthy social-network host, the front-end containers showed no outgoing sockets when sampled, because nothing was calling them; an undeclared edge expires ten minutes after its last traffic. A front end that is idle therefore has no edge until traffic arrives, which is correct behaviour but looks like a fault. Declared edges from the Compose file keep an idle link on the screen. Hard-coded project names blocked traffic; the traffic controller accepted only five named projects, so benchmark hosts with other names could not be driven. Unknown projects now get a generic workflow.

6.2.title: Analysis
6.2.text: What the evidence supports. Three results are robust: the fact-aware hybrid names the true cause more often than the rules on real systems (the paired interval excludes zero). The container facts are the single most valuable component (the ablation shows 19 and 16 points). And the learned propagation model discriminates better than fixed edge probabilities on observed cascades (AUROC 0.847 against 0.784). What did not work. Three claims that were expected to hold did not. The random walk is not statistically better than ranking by anomaly alone on these benchmarks. Learned directions do not beat the name rule when names exist. Onset-precedence re-ranking was neutral. These are reported because a pipeline that is honest about where it stops is more useful to an operator than one that is not. The simple rule z-score is a strong detector on its own, and the Isolation Forest earns its place through quietness and complementarity, not discrimination. The measurement bug. Before the ledger reader was fixed, every engine was scored on only part of the real faults (14 of 31 per system were hidden), and the outages of the hidden faults were counted as false alarms. That is why every number in this report uses all 62 faults, and why a regression test now guards the reader.

6.3.title: Discussion and Threats to Validity
6.3.text: Construct validity. Ground truth is the injector’s ledger, which records the structural root cause and the services that can be affected. Whether an affected service visibly changes depends on protection that the ledger does not model, so cascade recall serves as a lower bound on true propagation. The evidence weighting in Section 4.6.1 is not isolated by the offline benchmarks because the recordings do not retain edge evidence. Internal validity. The settings were chosen by the authors. On the synthetic track, they were chosen on a disjoint tuning split and scored once; on the real track, they were not tuned on a held-out system, so the real numbers are optimistic by an unmeasured margin. The two container facts were found by inspecting the real runs. External validity. Two real applications and one capture. Architecture independence is argued from the cross-system check and the synthetic topologies, not proven; the simulator is cleaner than a real system (for example, restarts do not lower memory in it). Conclusion validity: with 62 real faults, a difference below about eight points cannot be resolved, and overlapping faults make the intervals optimistic. A caution about auto-restart. The mapper can restart crashed containers on a target (Section 5.11 and Chapter 3). Evaluation runs should be made with auto-restart switched off, so that the mapper does not heal the faults the injector applies; the reader of this report should confirm the setting of any run they intend to repeat.

6.5.title: Significance and Implications
6.5.text: Three practical points follow. An instrumentation-free tool can recover a usable call graph and a useful ranking, and for small teams, that is the difference between having a diagnosis tool and not. Container facts are worth more than any statistical refinement: a stopped container is something one knows, and folding it into an anomaly score throws information away. The right operating contract for an alarm is the one the operator experiences, which is why alarm time is reported beside false-alarm episodes.

7.1.title: Summary of Work
7.1.text: The project built an instrumentation-free platform that watches containerised microservices from the outside, recovers their call graph, and runs an unsupervised diagnosis pipeline on it. A collector agent reads Docker state, statistics, and socket tables over SSH; an evidence-weighted graph orients each edge by its listening port; a hybrid detector combining per-service Isolation Forests and a robust rule layer treats container facts as evidence; a ranker splits each deviation into what neighbours explain and what they do not, and runs a random walk over the call graph; a cascade model with learned Beta–Binomial edge probabilities predicts who is next. A dashboard shows the result in 2D and 3D, and a Detection Engines page runs Rules, ML, and Hybrid in parallel, showing what each detected, computed, and predicted. The system was evaluated on 62 faults injected blind into two real containerised systems and on 178 held-out synthetic faults, and operated on further benchmark applications on EC2.

7.2.title: Conclusions
7.2.text: 1. On 62 real faults the hybrid names the true cause first for 74% against 65% for the rule layer (paired +9.7 points, 95% CI [+1.6,+17.7], p = 0.032); on the synthetic set the difference is not significant (+2.2 points). 2. The container facts are the most valuable single component: removing the "docker stop" fact costs 19 points on the real systems and 16 points on the synthetic set. 3. Learned propagation discriminates better than fixed edge probabilities on 80 observed cascades (AUROC 0.847 against 0.784), with a lower Brier score and a lower expected calibration error. On the real systems, the experiment is uninformative because almost no real fault cascaded. 4. Learned directions stay correct when service names carry no information (28 of 31 real pairs against none for the name rule), but they do not improve ranking when names exist. 5. Change-point alarms roughly halve the median detection delay on the real systems (10.5 s to 4.9 s), at the price of more alarm time (7% to 16%). CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE 6. The simple rule-based z-score is a strong detector on its own; the Isolation Forest earns its place as a complementary method. place through quietness and by complementing the rules. 7. The pipeline costs about 6 to 7 ms per five-second window on the systems tested, on one core, with no GPU. 8. A host too small for its workload looks like a mapper fault; the diagnostic tools separate the two.

7.3.title: Contributions
7.3.text: • An observation layer that recovers topology and direction from the host alone. • A probabilistic cascading-failure model with learned propagation. • A hybrid detector with an honest operating contract (alarm time as well as false-alarm rate) episodes). • A fact-aware, decomposition-based ranker and learned call directions. • A detection engines page showing three engines in parallel. • A blind, reproducible evaluation that includes the negative results and a corrected measurement bug. • A working platform with 329 automated tests, a traffic generator and host-diagnostic tools.

7.4.title: Utility and Applications
7.4.text: The platform provides a small team with a first-line diagnosis tool for Docker-based systems that nobody wants to instrument, a teaching and benchmarking harness for cascading failures, and a triage layer in front of heavier observability products (Chapter 6, Potential Applications).

7.5.title: Limitations
7.5.text: • Coarse signals. Eight metrics every five seconds. A brownout on an almost idle system. service never raises an alarm; no engine here catches it. • Two real systems. Architecture independence is argued from a cross-system check and synthetic topologies, not proven. Real cascades were too rare in the recordings to test learned propagation on real data. • Edge evidence is not isolated offline. The recordings do not retain edge evidence, so the effect of the evidence weighting is not measured. • No scaling measurement. The cost was measured at 12 and 13 services only. • Tuned by the authors. Real-system settings were not tuned on a held-out system, so those numbers are optimistic by an unmeasured margin. • Auto-restart. The mapper restarts crashed containers by default (switch off with MAPPER_AUTO_RESTART=off); runs meant to measure detection should have this feature switched off. • Default ingest token. The push endpoint has a built-in token, which must be changed when the server is reachable by others. • Not tested on Kubernetes, and the dashboard views were checked on a simulated target, not on every benchmark host.

7.6.title: Scope for Future Work
7.6.text: A larger measured campaign on more real systems, and a public labelled data set for comparability. • Real multi-service cascades to test learned propagation where it matters; promotion of learned directions and change-point alarms into the live system behind its operator switch. • Retention of edge evidence in the recordings, so that the evidence weighting can be isolated and measured. • A language-model agent on top of the structured evidence (cause, evidence, runbook) to answer follow-up questions or draft a change, with the evidence as its only grounding, evaluated through a user study; any action it proposes would go through an approval gate. • Support for Kubernetes through the same observation idea (node-level access to container sockets), and a scaling benchmark. • Brownout detection on idle services, perhaps with active probing of the service.
